title: Screen Addiction and Time Management Before Independence
summary: Before your child leaves for university or work, your gentle guidance will fade, and their habits will be their only guardian. Many intelligent teenagers stumble not due to lack of ability, but because screen addiction consumes their time. Help them now to build a self-governing system: conscious boundaries for social media and games, deep-focus periods without their phone, and understanding how apps are designed to steal their attention. The goal is not prohibition but control—so they use the tool, rather than being used by it. The skill they master now in managing their attention will determine their success when no one is watching.
try_this: This week: Help your child measure their actual screen time for 3 days (via phone settings), then let them set a goal and one daily period for deep focus without their phone.
reflection_prompts: Does your child have a self-governing system for time management that will endure when your *rifq* disappears?
Which single digital habit, if they regulated it now, would change their path toward independence?

review_defects.why: The Arabic says 'your supervision (رقابتك) disappears'. The translator replaced 'supervision' with the Islamic term 'rifq' (gentleness) and added an explanatory gloss, introducing a concept not present in the source. This changes the meaning from parental monitoring to a specific religious virtue.
Same error as in summary: 'رقابتك' (your supervision) is mistranslated as 'rifq'.

The Arabic consistently uses the masculine singular 'ابنك' (your son) and masculine pronouns, addressing parents of boys. The English generalizes to 'your child' and 'they', losing the specific gender reference.

review_defects.arabic: تختفي رقابتك وتبقى عادته هي حارسه الوحيد
review_defects.english: your *rifq* (gentle guidance) will fade, and their habits will be their only guardian
review_defects.why: The Arabic is direct and uses everyday language ('your supervision disappears'). The English inserts an Islamic term ('rifq') with a gloss, making the tone more preachy and clinical than the original warm, direct advice.
